title: Demonstrationes circa residua ex divisione potestatum per numeros primos resultantia

deep.reconstruction:
Setting: p = 2n+1 is prime and a is a primitive root, so ord_p(a) = 2n. Theorem 40 on the previous page proved a^n ≡ -1 (mod p). It argues that a^{2n} - 1 = (a^n - 1)(a^n + 1), and the first factor is not divisible by p because the order is minimal.

Corollary 1 (§41). Let 1, α, β, γ, ... be the residues of 1, a, a^2, a^3, ... (so α = a, β ≡ aα, γ ≡ aβ, ...). Then the residues of a^n, a^{n+1}, a^{n+2}, ... are -1, -α, -β, -γ, ..., that is 2n, 2n+1-α, 2n+1-β, .... In modern terms, a^{n+λ} ≡ -a^λ (mod p).

Corollary 2 (§42). The full period of 2n residues, before repetition, splits into two halves. The second half consists of the complements (negatives) of the first half: residue(a^λ) + residue(a^{n+λ}) ≡ 0 (mod p), i.e. the two residues sum to p.

Scholion (§43). Euler links this to his earlier 'socii' (pairs r, s with rs ≡ 1 mod p, i.e. modular inverses). In the cyclic list the two members of an inverse pair stand equidistant from the middle term a^n ≡ -1: a^{n+ν} · a^{n-ν} = a^{2n} ≡ 1. The middle residue -1 is its own inverse, just as +1 is. The next page adds that all other pairs consist of distinct elements, and that for any r coprime to p the inverse can be written s = (1 + m p)/r for suitable m.

Purpose: these are structural lemmas about the cyclic group (Z/pZ)^* generated by a primitive root. They lead into Theorem 44: the number of primitive roots equals φ(p-1).
errors: None of substance; the arguments are correct (assuming, as Euler does here, that a primitive root exists).

The claim that ±1 are the only self-inverse residues is implicit (it is equivalent to x^2 ≡ 1 having only the roots ±1 mod p) and is not proved on this page; Euler's earlier sections on 'socii' presumably cover it.

ideas.what: For a primitive root a mod p = 2n+1, a^{n+λ} ≡ -a^λ: the second half of the power cycle is the negative of the first half.
ideas.modern_name: g^{(p-1)/2} ≡ -1; the multiplication-by-(-1) symmetry of the cyclic group (Z/pZ)^*
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (E262, E449); systematized by Gauss, Disquisitiones Arithmeticae (1801), arts. 52-62
ideas.where_published: E449 itself (Novi Commentarii Acad. Sci. Petrop. 18, 1774); related material in E262 (Theoremata circa residua ex divisione potestatum relicta)

ideas.what: Modular inverse pairs (socii) correspond to exponents symmetric about n: a^{n+ν}·a^{n-ν} ≡ 1. Only ±1 are self-paired.
ideas.modern_name: Inverse of g^k is g^{p-1-k}; involution x -> x^{-1} on a cyclic group (the pairing behind the standard proof of Wilson's theorem)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler / Lagrange / Gauss (Wilson's theorem pairing argument)
ideas.where_published: E449 (earlier sections on residua socia); Gauss DA art. 77ff for Wilson's theorem via pairing

deep.surprise_reason: Standard, well-documented elementary facts about powers of a primitive root in Euler's known 1774 memoir. Nothing beyond what the literature attributes to Euler and Gauss.
transcription_corrections: 'cum ſit α = α' should read 'cum ſit α = a' (Latin a, the radix), i.e. α = a, β = aα, γ = aβ.
In §42 'et -1, -α, -β, -γ, - etc.' — the image shows '-γ, - etc.' (Euler's trailing dash), so the transcription is faithful.
